While effective at mitigating mutual interference between simultaneously operating sensors where colors match and at detecting common depths, these devices often struggle with deeper objects and multi-modal scenes when sensor colors differ and sampling rates vary due to changes in relative motion and geometry within the environment. Our core contributions include: (i) introducing torque as a shape-dependent metric for assessing depth sensor integrity and (ii) refining this dataset and release it to the community at no cost.

This paper addresses that gap by investigating the fundamental limits of recommendation during a specific turn-based recommendation protocol, assuming a stochastic user model. This protocol specifies that a reviewer begins each turn by presenting a query, prompting the recommendation system to suggest an item; upon observing whether that suggestion matched the target, a noise component modifies the query for the subsequent turn until the system's item budget is exhausted. This framework accommodates various sophisticated recommendation algorithms, allowing us to treat the solver as a generic black box. To analyze this setup, we define the instance as the collection of all user sessions and query sequences, characterizing both instance and pure learning metrics that respectively evaluate the system relative to its specific interaction with historical data or its accuracy on an unbiased test set. Our main contribution establishes several solve-dependent sample complexity lower bounds, revealing intrinsic limits of the solving process given limited query interactions. Complementary to these limits is an upper bound demonstrating that an optimal solving strategy exists with a success probability at least as strong as those parameters indicated; this strategy is referred to as the empirical process. Additionally, we introduce the concept of instance learning, successfully estimating lower bounds for specific datasets from within. Empirical validation using both synthetic generated and real-world user interaction logs confirms the tightness of our theoretical characterizations and verifies the efficacy of our proposed optimal solving method.

This study introduces a novel approach to detect TB by modeling airflow obstruction and distribution. First, an algorithm is presented to simultaneously measure airway expansion and airway ectasis based on the tree-like architecture of pulmonary bronchi. Second, combining this method with single-exhalation magnetic resonance (MR) joule imaging acquired during controlled abnormal breathing provides maps of expired ventilated fraction (EVF). This study introduces Human Uncomfortable Bright Regions, defining uncomfortable zones within an environment map from both physiological and psychological perspectives. It further proposes a quantitative index termed Human Comfortable Brightness Resolution to measure spatial detail of non-uncomfortable zones. These new metrics were validated using human subject tests across various maps. The study results show that proposed models correlate closely with human evaluation responses, outperforming existing comfortable viewing field and visual discomfort techniques. Additionally different algorithms were suggested for detecting and handling uncomfortable zones to improve future super environments applications in reality.
